newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seen starting full probe into BT/MCI deal.
newsitem.headline: EU seen starting full probe into BT/MCI deal.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to launch a full probe into the alliance between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp. later this week, EU sources said Wednesday.
"There is every chance that the deal will go into the second phase (of investigation)," a commission official said, but declined to give any details.

The planned $20 billion merger between the two telecommunications giants was submitted to the commission for clearance in December under the EU's merger rules, which ban creation or strengthening of dominant positions.

The commission has until Thursday to decide whether to clear it after its preliminary inquiry or launch an in-depth probe if it is worried about the impact on fair competition in Europe. Such a probe could last up to four months.

But whether the commission goes for that extra time seems to pose little danger to the alliance itself, which still faces its main regulatory challenge on the other side of the Atlantic, industry sources and antitrust lawyers said.
"I don't think there is going to be a problem about the transaction," said Peter Alexiadis, a partner with law firm Squire Sanders & Dempsey, which represents MCI in the United States.

Alexiadis warned against reading too much into the expected decision to open the full probe, adding that the commission may only need more time to assess whether British Telecom will be in a position to abuse its position in the British market, as some rival companies have argued.
AT&T Corp. has demanded that the approval of the operation be made subject to competitive safeguards and commitments regarding fair pricing and equal access to phone lines.

AT&T Media Relations Manager Niall Hickey stressed that British customers currently have to dial an extra three digits when making a call through his company compared with British Telecom, a problem he thought should be examined by the Commission.

Hickey also expressed concern that British Telecom may be offering MCI more favourable prices for accessing its network, something which should be prevented as long as British Telecom's network was indispensable for rival companies to offer their services.
British Telecom's Brussels office was not aware of the commission's intentions regarding the alliance, but expressed little surprise at the prospect of a thorough investigation.

"We are not picking up any negative vibes about the merger ... but there may be some nervousness because it is just so big," British Telecom's EU affairs official, Mike Corkerry, said in an interview.
Corkerry was optimistic the deal would be ultimately cleared in the EU as well as the United States.
Bell Atlantic Corp. is apparently the only company to have called for an outright ban of the merger, the sources said.

But it is in the United States that the deal will face its most important challenge because under the plan announced in November, British Telecom would take full control of MCI. That is forbidden under U.S. legislation unless the British market is found to be as open to competition as the American market.
British Telecom already has a 20 percent stake in MCI. The two companies are hoping to conclude their alliance this fall after clearing all regulatory hurdles.
